source.title: Make It Long, Keep It Fast: End-to-End 10K Long User Behavior Sequence Modeling for Billion-Scale Douyin Recommendation
source.authors: Lin Guan; Jia-Qi Yang; Zhi-Shan Zhao; Bei-Chuan Zhang; Bo Sun; Xuan-Yuan Luo; Ji-Nan Ni; Xiao-Wen Li; Yu-Hang Qi; Zhifang Fan; Hang-Yu Wang; Qi-Wei Chen; Yi Cheng; Feng Zhang; Xiao Yang

record.file_problem: None noted; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Applies and measures scaling-like behavior in a new setting: Douyin recommendation models, with sequence length and sequence-module capacity varied. It does not test language-model pretraining loss laws directly.
record.gate_note: The paper reports recommendation AUC and NLL results as sequence length, model capacity, and training-length settings change. These are results in recommendation, not held-out language-model pretraining cross-entropy. It does not fit or report power-law exponents. The cited original scaling-law papers are contextual references, not results from this study.
record.test_reason: The paper uses LLM scaling laws as framing and calls its gains 'scaling-law-like', but it fits no power law and measures no exponent. It also does not measure held-out pretraining loss against parameters, tokens or compute in the claim's sense. Its one genuine scaling measurement (Figure 1) is recommendation finish-AUC lift against user-history length and sequence-module size (6M/23M/133M). It shows only monotonic gains, so it cannot bear on V5's 'same power-law form'. Context length is also not one of the claim's scaling variables. The remaining results (Figure 3, Tables 3–5, Section 4.4) compare the authors' architecture and training regime with alternatives. The study reports no result on any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Essentially correct. The authors conclude that STCA, RLB and 'train sparsely, infer densely' together give monotonic, scaling-law-like gains with history length and sequence-module capacity. Sparse training recovers about 80% of the 10k-training gain at about one-third of the cost. STCA reaches similar NLL to Transformer at about 7.4× less sequence compute, and the system delivers significant online engagement gains on Douyin.
record.recipe_differences: This is a production recommender-system study, not an experiment using the language-model loss-scaling methods. It varies recommendation history length and sequence-module settings and reports AUC/NLL rather than held-out language-model pretraining cross-entropy.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with sequence length, sequence-module capacity, maximum and average training length, and training-length sampling choices.

fits_no_version.finding: In Douyin finish prediction, AUC lift rises monotonically with user-history length (500 to 10k tokens) and with sequence-module size (6M, 23M, 133M parameters). The largest model shows smaller gains from 8k to 10k. No functional form is fitted.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Recommendation ranking quality improves monotonically with history length and sequence-module parameters (scaling-like behaviour without a tested power law).

record.peer_reviewed: ACM Web Conference 2026 (WWW '26), as stated in the paper
record.problems: The scaling results are for recommendation metrics rather than language-model pretraining loss. The paper does not fit power laws or report scaling exponents; several plotted values are available only as figures.
record.rows_left_out: No other results relevant to the scaling analogy were left out. General architecture ablations, business-metric results, and system-efficiency measurements are not rows because they do not measure the scaling behavior named by the claim.

untested.parts: Held-out LM pretraining loss as a power law in parameters, tokens or compute.
Extrapolation from small fitted runs to much larger ones.
Architecture shape at fixed parameter count. Table 2's ablations change components and parameter counts together, at 512 tokens.
Whether a power-law form holds in recommendation. Only monotonic gains are reported, with no fit or exponent.
Downstream predictability from LM scale or loss.
Dependence of fitted exponents on fitting choices; deviation from a single power law.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T3' with a V5 limits_scope label is not supported. A missing power-law fit is an untested part of V5, not a limit on its scope, and most rows are ablations or comparisons of the authors' own method. The scaling-law papers are cited only as motivation.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss versus parameter count, training tokens, or training compute.
Prediction of much larger language-model runs from power laws fitted on small runs.
Compute-optimal language-model parameter/token allocation and its scaling with compute.
Architecture variation at fixed language-model parameter count.

The paper reports analogous recommendation scaling results, but does not fit or establish the same power-law form or estimate exponents. It does not test the listed image/video, repeated-data, fine-tuning, or transfer settings.
Downstream-task predictability from language-model scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of fitted language-model exponents or compute-optimal allocations on fitting choices, or bending away from a single power law.

relation.reason: The introduction, abstract and conclusion explicitly compare monotonic recommendation gains with scaling-law behavior, but the experiments do not test the catalog's claim versions.

tranche.reason: The paper reports recommendation quality and system efficiency, without testing a power-law form, fitted extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, or downstream predictability from pretraining scale or loss. Scaling laws supply framing rather than an operational tool.

source_check.notes: The numerical rows and authors-conclusion paraphrase agree with the supplied text; none supplies evidence for a claim-version verdict. The source is arXiv v3 dated 19 May 2026 with a revised title and a 2026 ACM reference, whereas the pack lists year 2025.

reader_labels.condition: Douyin recommendation experiments reported in Figures 1 and 3 and Tables 3 and 4
reader_labels.reason: The reported results show monotonic or increasing recommendation metrics across tested scale settings, but do not fit or establish a common power-law form; see r1-r12.
